docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: PandoraBox is an open source USB decontamination kiosk, a "sheep-dip station": a user inserts a USB key, the kiosk scans every file with several detection engines, shows the dangerous files it found, and removes them when the user touches the screen. It is a complete rewrite of the first version of PandoraBox, without dependency on Pandora (CIRCL).

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
USB keys remain a common way into information systems that are otherwise well protected: shared between organizations, used on unmanaged computers, plugged into isolated networks. A decontamination kiosk checks them before they are used on a workstation.

PandoraBox aims to be a free, auditable and hardened alternative to commercial kiosks, for sensitive environments: healthcare, industry, public administration. It runs on a refurbished small computer with a touch screen, and works without network.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Several engines: known malicious hashes (MalwareBazaar), known files (CIRCL Hashlookup), ClamAV, YARA-X rules (YARA Forge) and structure heuristics (programs disguised as documents, PDF with JavaScript). See Detection engines.
  • Fail closed: a file that could not be fully scanned (encrypted archive, limit exceeded, engine error) is never reported as clean. Every partition of a key is scanned; a partition that cannot be (encrypted, unknown filesystem) makes the key not verified.
  • Nothing is removed without the user: the dangerous files are listed on the screen, copied to the quarantine of the kiosk, then removed from the key only after a touch of the screen.
  • Traceability: every scan produces a structured JSON report.

docs.title: Guiding principles
docs.text:
• Minimal, hardened image: the system contains only what is needed to scan. Read-only root filesystem with dm-verity, Secure Boot, USBGuard, no account and no login. See Image internals.
  • Defense in depth: the USB key is hostile, and the analyzers are assumed to be compromisable. Each engine runs in its own sandbox, without network.
  • Offline by default: no network is needed to scan; signatures and system updates come on signed USB keys, or through a dedicated online channel. See Signatures.
  • Customizable: the organization sets its logo, colors and texts of the interface. See Interface.

docs.title: Building the image
docs.text:
The kiosk is a complete system image, built with mkosi from Debian 13 (trixie) packages. Everything runs in a Debian 13 container (image/Dockerfile: mkosi, QEMU, OVMF): the build computer only needs Docker.

Warning

The image and the signature sets are signed with development keys only. The production image has no signature set: the kiosk scans nothing until a signature update device is inserted (see Signatures). See the phase 2 tasks in the roadmap.

docs.title: In short
docs.text:
image/build.sh                     # offline kiosk
image/build.sh --profile online    # kiosk with network: online updates, SIEM, NTP

The image is image/mkosi.output/pandora-box.raw: write it to the disk of the kiosk (Initial installation), or test it first in a virtual machine (Testing with QEMU).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Docker, about 5 GB of disk space, network access (Debian packages and Python wheels).

docs.title: Before the build
docs.text:
The image is read-only: everything below is part of it, and changing it means building a new image, then installing it as an update.

What Where Configuration of the kiosk packaging/pandora-box.toml (see Configuration) Theme of the interface image/theme/ (see Interface) Mode of the screen video= on the kernel command line, image/mkosi.conf (see Screen) Touchscreen allowed by USBGuard image/mkosi.extra/etc/usbguard/rules.conf (see USB devices) Disk controller of another computer KernelModulesInitrdInclude= of image/mkosi.conf (see Unified kernel image) Certificate authorities of the SIEM image/siem-ca.pem (see SIEM) abuse.ch Auth-Key, profile online image/credentials.toml (see Profile online) NTP servers, profile online see Time

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
The image is signed with image/mkosi.key and image/mkosi.crt (systemd-boot, unified kernel image, dm-verity root hash): the firmware of a kiosk only starts an image signed with this key. It trusts the signature sets, image updates and maintenance requests signed with image/update.key: its public key image/update.pem is installed in the image.

When they do not exist, image/build.sh generates a development pair of each, valid 10 years, that never leaves the build computer (ignored by git). Keep them: a kiosk only accepts the updates signed with the keys of its image. A kiosk must only trust the release keys of the project, which are not defined yet: they will be kept out of the repository, and mkosi can sign with a key in a hardware token (--secure-boot-key-source=provider:pkcs11).

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
image/build.sh                  # production image
image/build.sh --profile online # production image with network
image/build.sh --profile test   # test image, for the virtual machine only

The image is written to image/mkosi.output/: pandora-box.raw (or pandora-box-test.raw, a GPT disk image), the unified kernel image (.efi) and the list of installed packages (.manifest). The first build takes a few minutes; the following ones reuse the installed packages (mkosi incremental build, cached in the pandora-box-mkosi Docker volume) and take less than a minute.

The cache is not rebuilt when image/requirements.txt or image/mkosi.prepare.chroot change: rebuild it with image/build.sh -f (docker volume rm pandora-box-mkosi removes it completely).

The version of the image is the date and time of its build, UTC, like the serial of a signature set: 20261005143700 (--image-version=N overrides it). It is in /etc/os-release (IMAGE_VERSION), in the labels of its partitions and in the name of its unified kernel image. An update must have a newer version than the running one.

docs.title: Profile online
docs.text:
Without a profile, the image has no network configuration at all. --profile online adds online signature updates from their sources (see Signatures): systemd-networkd (DHCP on the wired network), systemd-resolved, systemd-timesyncd, freshclam, the pandora-box-update timer and a firewall that only lets the update service, the log export to a SIEM (see SIEM) and NTP out (image/mkosi.profiles/online/). Its postinst.chroot enables [updates] in the configuration of the kiosk, and installs the credentials of image/credentials.toml (outside git) in /etc/credstore.

cp image/credentials.toml.example image/credentials.toml   # then the abuse.ch Auth-Key
image/build.sh --profile online

Warning

An image built with credentials must not be published: anyone with the image or the disk of the kiosk can read them.

docs.title: Time
docs.text:
The clock of the kiosk dates its logs and scan reports, and decides whether the certificates of the update servers and of the SIEM are valid. An online kiosk synchronizes it with systemd-timesyncd, from the NTP servers of NTP= in image/mkosi.profiles/online/mkosi.extra/usr/lib/systemd/timesyncd.conf.d/50-pandora-box.conf (empty by default), else those the DHCP server gives, else the Debian pool (FallbackNTP=). To use the servers of the organization, set them there before building the image:

[Time]
NTP=ntp1.example.org ntp2.example.org

Only systemd-timesyncd may send NTP requests (UDP 123) through the firewall; timedatectl timesync-status shows the server in use. NTP is not authenticated (timesyncd has no NTS): someone in the path of the requests can shift the clock, so prefer NTP servers of the local network. Without the profile, the kiosk keeps the time of its hardware clock (UTC).

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Runtime dependencies are pinned with their hashes in image/requirements.txt. After a change of the dependencies in pyproject.toml, regenerate it with image/lock-requirements.sh, then rebuild the cache (image/build.sh -f).

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
Path Role image/mkosi.conf Image definition: Debian 13, x86_64, systemd-boot, unified kernel image (UKI), packages image/mkosi.repart/ Partitions: ESP, two system slots (read-only root filesystem, its dm-verity hash and signature), data partition image/mkosi.images/initrd/ The initrd: the default initrd of mkosi, which restarts instead of opening an emergency shell, without the files a read-only root does not need image/mkosi.prepare.chroot Runtime dependencies in a virtual environment (/usr/lib/pandora-box), from image/requirements.txt (pinned with their hashes) image/mkosi.build.chroot pandora-box wheel, built from the repository without network image/mkosi.postinst.chroot Installs pandora-box, its configuration, systemd service, tmpfiles and logrotate files (packaging/), and the clamd settings image/mkosi.extra/ Files copied into the image: systemd presets (enabled and disabled units), /etc/fstab, growth of the data partition (/usr/lib/repart.d/), A/B updates (/usr/lib/sysupdate.d/, boot assessment), USBGuard policy, kernel settings (sysctl.d), firewall (nftables.conf), clamd sandbox image/mkosi.profiles/online/ Profile online image/mkosi.profiles/test/ Test profile, for the virtual machine tests only image/vm/ Virtual machine tests: corpus, QEMU driver, automated test image/build.sh, image/vm.sh Build and run in the container image/build-test.sh, image/package-update.sh Build the images of the virtual machine test; build a signed image update image/maintenance-key.sh Prepare a maintenance device

What the image contains and how it is protected: see Image internals.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The kiosk reads its configuration from /etc/pandora-box/pandora-box.toml (another file with --config, or the PANDORA_BOX_CONFIG environment variable). Every key is optional: a missing key takes its default value. The configuration is checked at startup, and an unknown key or an invalid value is refused: the kiosk does not start with a configuration it does not understand.

In the image, the root filesystem is read-only: the configuration is part of the image, taken from packaging/pandora-box.toml when the image is built. To change it, edit that file, build a new image and install it as an update (see Building the image and System updates).

Check a configuration, its signatures, its engines and its theme without starting the kiosk:

pandora-box --config pandora-box.toml --check-config

docs.title: Sections
docs.text: Section Settings [kiosk] Name of the kiosk in the logs, interface (framebuffer, curses, console), FAKE_SCAN mode [display] Theme, language, framebuffer, return to the waiting screen: see Interface [device] Mount point, allowed filesystems, eject [scan] Parallel workers, timeout per file, suspicious and on_error policies, sandbox [limits] Maximum file size, number of files, folder depth [policy] Number of engines needed for a malicious verdict [engines.*] Each detection engine: see Detection engines [signatures] Signature sets and their verification: see Signatures [updates] Online signature and image updates: see Signatures and System updates [siem] Log export to a SIEM: see Log export to a SIEM [report], [quarantine], [logging] Folders of the scan reports, of the quarantine, log file and level: see Logs

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
The configuration of the image, packaging/pandora-box.toml, with every key, its default value and its meaning:

# PandoraBox configuration
# Installed as /etc/pandora-box/pandora-box.toml. Every key is optional:
# the values below are the defaults. Unknown keys are rejected at startup.
# Check this file with: pandora-box --check-config

[kiosk]
# Kiosk name written in every log entry (default: host name)
# name = "kiosk-01"

# FAKE_SCAN mode, for development only: no real detection is performed,
# only the EICAR test file is reported as malicious.
fake_scan = false

# User interface: "framebuffer" (graphical, touch screen), "curses" (full
# screen text, administrator mode) or "console" (plain text)
interface = "framebuffer"

[display]
# Graphical interface (kiosk.interface = "framebuffer"). Theme folder: logo,
# colors, texts and images in place of the built-in ones ("" for the built-in
# theme, the default). In the image, the files of image/theme/: see
# docs/interface.md.
theme = "/usr/share/pandora-box/theme"
# Language of the texts: "en", "fr", or a language the theme adds
language = "en"
# Framebuffer device
framebuffer = "/dev/fb0"
# A result stays on the screen until the device is removed, then this long
# (seconds) before the waiting screen
return_seconds = 5.0

[device]
# Folder where the USB device is mounted (must exist)
mount_point = "/media/pandora-box"

# Mounting a block device requires root (CAP_SYS_ADMIN): adding the user to a
# group is not enough. Run the kiosk as root (systemd service), or set
# use_sudo = true to run mount/umount through "sudo -n", with a sudoers rule
# limited to these commands, for instance:
#   pandora-box ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/mount, /usr/bin/umount, /usr/bin/eject
use_sudo = false

# Filesystems that may be mounted; any other device is rejected
allowed_filesystems = ["vfat", "exfat", "ntfs", "ext4"]

# Timeout of mount/umount commands, in seconds
command_timeout = 60

# Eject the device (/usr/bin/eject, Debian package "eject") when the scan and
# the cleaning are over, so that the user can remove it safely. While the
# user is asked to confirm the cleaning, the device is only unmounted.
eject = true

# DEVELOPMENT ONLY, never on a kiosk: when the desktop mounts USB devices
# itself (udisks automount), use that mount instead of mounting the device.
# The device is then scanned on the system mount (usually read-write, maybe
# without noexec) and mount_point is ignored. It is unmounted and mounted
# again with udisksctl, which the desktop user may run without root.
auto_mount = false
# Maximum time to wait for the system to mount the device, in seconds
auto_mount_wait = 15.0

[scan]
# Number of files scanned in parallel: "auto" (one per CPU, as many as the
# memory allows: 1.5 GB for clamd and the system, then 256 MB each, for the
# YARA rules mostly), or a number
workers = "auto"

# Maximum time to scan one file with all the engines, in seconds. A worker
# that exceeds it is killed and the file is reported as an error.
file_timeout = 300.0

# Files reported as suspicious by an engine:
#   "block": quarantined and removed from the device, like malicious files
#   "warn":  kept on the device, the user is warned
suspicious = "block"

# Files that could not be fully scanned (engine error or timeout, file over a
# limit, too many files or folders too deep):
#   "block": the device is reported as NOT VERIFIED and must not be used
#            (unscanned files are listed but never removed)
#   "warn":  the user is warned and the unscanned files are listed
on_error = "block"

# FAKE_SCAN mode only: simulated scan time per file, in seconds
fake_delay = 0.0

# Run each scan worker in a sandbox: bubblewrap (no network, a minimal file
# system without the device), as sandbox_user without privileges, with a
# system call filter. The kiosk opens the files and passes them to the
# workers. Needs root, bwrap and setpriv: set it to false for development.
sandbox = true
sandbox_user = "pandora-box-scan"

[limits]
# Files bigger than this size (in bytes) are not scanned (default: 1 GiB)
max_file_size = 1073741824
# Maximum number of files on a device; the scan stops beyond it
max_files = 100000
# Maximum folder depth; deeper folders are not scanned
max_depth = 64

[policy]
# Number of engines that must report a file as malicious; with fewer
# positive engines, the file is only suspicious
min_malicious_engines = 1

# Detection engines. Every engine is enabled unless explicitly disabled:
# if an enabled engine cannot load its signatures, the kiosk refuses to start.
# At least one content engine (clamav or yara) is required.
# Signature updates come with phase 2: see docs/engines.md.

[engines.malwarebazaar]
# Offline list of malicious SHA-256 hashes (abuse.ch MalwareBazaar),
# converted with: python -m pandora_box.hashdb build <export> <database>
enabled = true
database = "/var/lib/pandora-box-signatures/current/malwarebazaar/malwarebazaar.sha256.bin"

[engines.hashlookup]
# CIRCL hashlookup Bloom filter of known files (SHA-1, DCSO bloom format).
# "Known" does not mean "benign", and a Bloom filter has false positives
# (about 1 in 10,000): see docs/engines.md.
enabled = true
bloom = "/var/lib/pandora-box-signatures/current/hashlookup/hashlookup-full.bloom"
# Do not run ClamAV and YARA on known files (malicious hashes are always
# checked). Off: known is not benign, the CIRCL filter also lists the EICAR
# test file, tools and malware; on only saves time on software devices
skip_content_engines = false
# The filter is published monthly
max_age_days = 45.0

[engines.clamav]
# clamd Unix socket. clamd.conf must set "AlertExceedsMax yes": otherwise
# clamd reports content beyond its limits as clean without scanning it.
enabled = true
socket = "/run/clamav/clamd.ctl"
# "fildes": pass the open file to clamd, "instream": send its content,
# "auto": fildes, then instream if clamd cannot use the descriptor
mode = "auto"
# Socket timeout for one file, in seconds
timeout = 120.0
# Must not exceed MaxFileSize, MaxScanSize and StreamMaxLength of clamd.conf:
# bigger files are reported as errors without being sent (default: 100 MiB)
max_file_size = 104857600
# Detection names reported as suspicious instead of malicious (documents
# with macros: Heuristics.OLE2.ContainsMacros, clamd.conf AlertOLE2Macros)
suspicious_names = ["PUA.*", "Heuristics.*"]
# Detection names meaning that the file was not fully scanned: beyond the
# limits of clamd (archives too, decompression bombs), encrypted archives and
# documents (clamd.conf AlertEncrypted)
error_names = ["Heuristics.Limits.Exceeded.*", "Heuristics.Encrypted.*"]

[engines.yara]
enabled = true
# Rule sets: a .yar file or a folder of .yar/.yara files, each in its own
# namespace. YARA Forge already includes the signature-base rules; to add the
# full signature-base set anyway, append:
#   { name = "signature-base", path = "/var/lib/pandora-box-signatures/current/yara/signature-base/yara" }
rules = [
    { name = "yara-forge", path = "/var/lib/pandora-box-signatures/current/yara/yara-forge/yara-rules-core.yar" },
]
# Compiled rules cache ("" disables it)
cache_dir = "/var/cache/pandora-box/yara"
# Scan timeout for one file, in seconds
timeout = 60.0
# Rules that do not compile:
#   "fail":      refuse to start
#   "skip_rule": ignore them; they are listed in the logs and every scan report
on_compile_error = "fail"
# Rule files to ignore (glob patterns matched against the file path)
exclude = []
# Rule "score" metadata (0-100): from malicious_score the file is malicious,
# from suspicious_score it is suspicious, below it the match is informational.
# default_score applies to rules without a score.
malicious_score = 75
suspicious_score = 40
default_score = 60


[engines.heuristics]
# Structure of the files, without signatures: PDF with JavaScript or a
# Launch action, programs disguised as documents (facture.pdf, facture.pdf.exe).
# Findings are suspicious.
enabled = true
[signatures]
# Warn at startup when a signature database is older than this (in days);
# each engine can override it with its own max_age_days. A database without
# a date (ClamAV custom signatures only) is logged, not shown.
max_age_days = 7.0

# Signed signature sets (docs/signatures.md). The engines read the files of
# the installed set, folder/current. A set is only installed when it is
# signed by a public key of the keys folder (*.pem) and newer than the
# installed one.
folder = "/var/lib/pandora-box-signatures"
keys = "/usr/share/pandora-box/keys"
# Verify the installed set at startup (signature and every file), and refuse
# engine files outside of it. Without a valid set, the kiosk does not scan:
# it only accepts a signature update device. Set it to false for development.
verify = true
# Install the signed set of a device that holds a pandora-box-signatures
# folder at its root (such a device is not scanned)
update_from_devices = true

[updates]
# Online signature updates (docs/signatures.md): off by default, a kiosk works
# offline. They also need the image profile "online" (network, firewall, and
# the pandora-box-update timer, every 6 hours).
enabled = false
# Either the kiosk downloads the signatures from their sources and signs
# the set with its own key (MalwareBazaar needs an abuse.ch Auth-Key, a
# credential of the image: docs/signatures.md)...
sources = []
# e.g. sources = ["clamav", "yara-forge", "malwarebazaar", "hashlookup"]
# ...or it downloads a published signed set: the folder of the set
# (manifest.json, its signature and the files). HTTPS is recommended, HTTP is
# accepted.
url = ""
# URLs in place of the default ones of the sources, e.g. a company mirror:
# mirrors = { clamav = "https://clamav.example.org", hashlookup = "https://..." }
# Folder of a published image update (A/B updates, docs/update.md); "" for
# no online image updates
image_url = ""
# HTTP(S) proxy, e.g. "http://proxy.example.org:3128" ("": direct)
proxy = ""
# Timeout of each request, in seconds
timeout = 300.0
# Install the signed image update of a device that holds a pandora-box-image
# folder at its root, then restart (A/B updates, docs/update.md)
image_from_devices = true

[siem]
# Export of the logs to a SIEM (docs/siem.md): off by default, a kiosk works
# offline. It also needs the image profile "online" (network, firewall, and
# the pandora-box-siem service). Every entry of the log file is sent, also
# those logged while the SIEM could not be reached.
enabled = false
# Host name or IP address of the SIEM
host = ""
# "tls" (certificate verified), "tcp" or "udp"
transport = "tls"
# Port of the SIEM; 0: 6514 for tls, 514 for tcp and udp
port = 0
# Certificate authorities of the SIEM certificate (PEM file), for tls; ""
# for those of the system. In the image: image/siem-ca.pem, installed as
# /usr/share/pandora-box/siem-ca.pem
ca = ""
# "syslog": RFC 5424 message, the JSON entry as message (octet counting over
# tcp and tls); "json": the JSON entry alone (one per line over tcp and tls)
format = "syslog"
# Syslog facility: "user" or "local0" to "local7"
facility = "local0"
# Timeout of the connection and of each send, in seconds
timeout = 10.0

[report]
# JSON scan reports, one per scanned device
folder = "/var/lib/pandora-box/reports"

[quarantine]
# Copy infected files to the kiosk before removing them from the device
enabled = true
folder = "/var/lib/pandora-box/quarantine"

[logging]
# JSON lines log file ("" disables logging)
file = "/var/log/pandora-box/pandora-box.log"
# DEBUG, INFO, WARNING or ERROR
level = "INFO"

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
This page explains how to work on PandoraBox on a development computer: run the kiosk outside the image, with or without real engines, and run the tests. To build the kiosk image and test it in a virtual machine, see Building the image and Testing with QEMU.

The code is in the pandora_box package (src/pandora_box/):

Module Role cli.py Command line entry point (pandora-box) config.py TOML configuration, validated at startup statemachine.py, kiosk.py State machine and kiosk workflow monitor.py USB detection with udev device.py Hardened mounting (ro,noexec,nosuid,nodev, read-write only to clean) inventory.py Device inventory: never follows links, never leaves the device, limits scanner.py, workers.py, worker.py Scan in supervised worker processes, timeouts and watchdog sigsets.py, publish.py Signed signature sets: verification, installation, publication from the sources, pandora-box-signatures command sandbox.py, seccomp.py, protocol.py Worker sandbox (bubblewrap, dedicated user, system call filter), validated JSON messages from the workers pipeline.py, hashing.py, filetype.py Per file: hashes (SHA-256, SHA-1, MD5), libmagic type, engines engines/ Engine interface, MalwareBazaar, Hashlookup, ClamAV, YARA-X and fake engine hashdb.py, bloom.py, clamd.py MalwareBazaar database, DCSO Bloom filter reader, clamd client policy.py Verdict aggregation per file and per device report.py, schemas/ JSON scan report and its JSON Schema signatures.py Signature provenance and freshness quarantine.py Copy of infected files with a manifest referencing the report imageupdate.py, maintenance.py A/B image updates, maintenance devices (log export) ui/ Graphical kiosk interface (framebuffer, themes), curses (administrator) and console interfaces logs.py, lock.py JSON logs, single-instance lock

Deployment files are in packaging/: configuration, systemd services, tmpfiles, sysusers and logrotate.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Linux with udev (USB detection and mounting require root privileges)
  • Python 3.11 or later
  • libmagic (sudo apt install libmagic1)
  • for real scans: clamav-daemon (see docs/engines.md)

Recent distributions (Debian 12 and later, Ubuntu 23.04 and later) forbid pip install into the system Python (PEP 668, externally-managed-environment error). Always work inside a virtual environment, and never use --break-system-packages.

docs.title: Create the virtual environment
docs.text:
If your system Python is 3.11 or later (Debian 12 and 13, Ubuntu 24.04):

sudo apt install python3-venv python3-full
git clone https://github.com/sourcentis/pandora-box.git
cd pandora-box
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -U pip
pip install -e ".[dev]"

If your system Python is older (Ubuntu 22.04 ships Python 3.10), use uv, which downloads a suitable Python without touching the system:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
git clone https://github.com/sourcentis/pandora-box.git
cd pandora-box
uv venv --python 3.11
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -e ".[dev]"

docs.title: Configure and run
docs.text:
cp packaging/pandora-box.toml pandora-box.toml
# YARA rules, MalwareBazaar (needs ABUSECH_AUTH_KEY), Hashlookup: an unsigned set
pandora-box-signatures publish dev-signatures --sources yara-forge,malwarebazaar,hashlookup
# copy the printed [engines.*] and [signatures] settings into pandora-box.toml,
# set the quarantine, report and log folders, then check the configuration
pandora-box --config pandora-box.toml --check-config
sudo .venv/bin/pandora-box --config pandora-box.toml --interface console

sudo resets PATH, so the kiosk is started with the full path of the executable installed in the virtual environment (.venv/bin/pandora-box).

Mounting a device requires root: adding your user to a group (such as disk) is not enough. On a desktop that mounts USB devices itself (udisks automount), set auto_mount = true in [device] instead: the kiosk then uses the system mount, and unmounts and mounts the device again with udisksctl, so it runs without sudo. This is for development only: the system mount is usually read-write and not hardened.

The device is unmounted while the kiosk asks the user to confirm the cleaning, so that it can be removed safely. To clean, it is mounted again read-write; a file is only removed if its SHA-256 is still the one that was scanned (another device may have been inserted in the meantime). When the scan and the cleaning are over, the device is ejected (device.eject, with eject, or udisksctl power-off in auto-mount mode).

The scan workers run in a sandbox by default (scan.sandbox): it needs root, bwrap (Debian package bubblewrap), setpriv and a pandora-box-scan user (sudo systemd-sysusers packaging/sysusers/pandora-box.conf). For development without them, set sandbox = false in [scan].

The kiosk only uses a signed signature set (signatures.verify, see docs/signatures.md): development signatures are not signed, set verify = false in [signatures] to use them.

To work on the workflow without signatures, set fake_scan = true in [kiosk] (or use --fake-scan): only the EICAR test file is reported as malicious, so the whole workflow (scan, quarantine, cleaning) can be tested without real engines.

docs.title: Lint and tests
docs.text:
With the virtual environment activated:

ruff check .
mypy src
pytest

Integration tests run against real engines when they are available: a clamd socket (PANDORA_BOX_CLAMD_SOCKET, default /run/clamav/clamd.ctl), real rules (PANDORA_BOX_YARA_RULES, paths separated by :) or a full configuration for the detection corpus (PANDORA_BOX_CORPUS_CONFIG). End-to-end tests with loop devices and a real clamd run in a container: tests/e2e/run.sh.

docs.title: Interface without a kiosk
docs.text:
The screens of the graphical interface can be drawn into PNG files, with made-up files, to work on them or on a theme without a framebuffer (see Interface):

pandora-box-theme preview /tmp/preview --language fr

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
This documentation is built with MkDocs and the Material theme, from the docs/ folder and mkdocs.yml. It is published on GitHub Pages by the docs workflow when docs/ changes on the main branch. To see it while writing:

pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
mkdocs serve        # http://127.0.0.1:8000, reloaded on every change
mkdocs build --strict

With MkDocs installed by pipx, add the extensions of requirements-docs.txt to its environment instead (the GitHub alerts, > [!WARNING], need markdown-callouts):

pipx install mkdocs
pipx inject mkdocs mkdocs-material markdown-callouts

docs.title: Detection engines and verdict policy
docs.text:
This document describes the phase 1 scanning pipeline: each detection engine, its data files and how to obtain them for development, and how verdicts are decided.

Warning

Signature downloads described here are for development only: these files are not signed. A kiosk only uses a signed signature set, verified at each start and installed from a signature update device: see signatures.md.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
For each inserted device:

  1. Inventory (kiosk process, metadata only): the mount point is walked with os.scandir/lstat. Links are never followed, the walk never leaves the device, and FIFOs, sockets and device files are listed as skipped. The limits apply here (see Limits).
  2. Scan (worker processes, one file at a time per worker):
  3. open the file read-only, component by component with O_NOFOLLOW, and check that it is the regular file the inventory recorded;
  4. compute SHA-256, SHA-1 and MD5 in a single streaming read;
  5. identify the type with libmagic (MIME type and description);
  6. run the hash engines (MalwareBazaar, then Hashlookup);
  7. run the content engines (ClamAV, YARA-X), unless the file is a known file and no hash engine reports it (see Hashlookup);
  8. aggregate the engine results into the file verdict.
  9. Device verdict, cleaning, and the JSON scan report.

Engines receive a FileInfo (relative path, size, hashes, MIME type, description and a read-only file descriptor). They never reopen the file by path and keep no state between files.

docs.title: Engines
docs.text:
Every engine is enabled by default. If an enabled engine cannot load its data, the kiosk refuses to start (pandora-box --check-config shows why). At least one content engine (ClamAV or YARA-X) is required: hash lookups alone only recognize files that are already known.

For development, pandora-box-signatures publish dev-signatures --sources yara-forge,malwarebazaar,hashlookup downloads the YARA rules, the MalwareBazaar list and the Hashlookup filter into ./dev-signatures/, checks them, and prints the matching configuration (an unsigned set: see signatures.md).

docs.title: MalwareBazaar
docs.text:
Offline list of SHA-256 hashes of known malware, from abuse.ch MalwareBazaar. A match is malicious (detection MalwareBazaar.KnownMalware).

  • Input: the full SHA-256 export. Downloading it requires a free abuse.ch Auth-Key (auth.abuse.ch), sent in the Auth-Key HTTP header, from https://bazaar.abuse.ch/export/txt/sha256/full/. The export is a zip archive holding full_sha256.txt: a # comment header, then one lower case hexadecimal SHA-256 per line. The converter accepts the zip archive or the text file. Any other line is an error: a malformed export is never partially loaded. In October 2026, the export held 1.1 million hashes, a 37 MB database.
  • Conversion: python -m pandora_box.hashdb build full_sha256.zip malwarebazaar.sha256.bin (python -m pandora_box.hashdb info <database> describes a database).
  • Format (pandora_box/hashdb.py): a 64-byte header (magic, version, count, creation time, SHA-256 of the source export) followed by the sorted 32-byte digests. The file is memory-mapped and searched by bisection: one million hashes take 32 MB, shared by the workers through the page cache.
  • Configuration: [engines.malwarebazaar] database.

docs.title: Hashlookup (CIRCL)
docs.text:
The CIRCL hashlookup Bloom filter of known files (NSRL, Linux distributions, software repositories).

  • Data: https://cra.circl.lu/hashlookup/hashlookup-full.bloom (about 1 GB and 418 million hashes in October 2026, updated monthly). It holds the SHA-1 of every known file, in upper case hexadecimal, in the DCSO bloom format.
  • Format: the format of the DCSO bloom Go tool and of the flor Python library. flor loads the whole bit array in memory (1 GB per worker), so PandoraBox has its own memory-mapped reader (pandora_box/bloom.py). The tests check that it agrees with flor. Against the real CIRCL filter, it agrees with flor, finds most Debian system binaries, and answers "known" for about 1 in 10,000 random hashes, as expected.
  • Known is not benign: the sources of hashlookup also contain offensive and dual-use tools. A Hashlookup hit is reported as the fact known = true with the verdict clean (no detection), never as a proof of safety.
  • False positives: a Bloom filter answers "known" for some unknown files. The CIRCL filter is built for a probability of 1 in 10,000. The probability is recorded with each answer (fp_rate) in the scan report.
  • Content engines on known files: by default, ClamAV and YARA-X scan every file, known or not. The CIRCL filter lists the files it has seen, among them the EICAR test file, offensive tools and malware samples: a kiosk that skipped them reported EICAR clean. [engines.hashlookup] skip_content_engines = true skips the content engines on known files, which saves time on devices full of common software, at that cost. The hash engines always run, and a MalwareBazaar match always wins: content engines still run on a known file that a hash engine reports. The skipped engines appear in the report with the reason known file (hashlookup), so the decision is auditable.

docs.title: ClamAV
docs.text:
ClamAV through the clamd daemon, with a small built-in client for its Unix socket protocol (pandora_box/clamd.py): zPING, zVERSION, zFILDES and zINSTREAM.

  • Modes ([engines.clamav] mode): fildes passes the open file descriptor to clamd, which therefore does not need to read the mount point; instream sends the content; auto (default) uses fildes, and instream only when clamd reports an error with the descriptor.
  • Verdicts: a detection is malicious, or suspicious when its name matches suspicious_names (default PUA.*, Heuristics.*). Names matching error_names (default Heuristics.Limits.Exceeded.*) mean that the file was not fully scanned: they are errors. INSTREAM size limit errors, timeouts and unexpected replies are errors too.
  • Versions: the engine version, the database version and its date come from VERSION, asked again for each scan report (clamd reloads its databases while running).

Required clamd.conf settings:

LocalSocket /run/clamav/clamd.ctl
# Without it, content beyond the limits below is reported as clean
# without being scanned
AlertExceedsMax yes
# At least engines.clamav.max_file_size (100 MiB by default)
MaxFileSize 100M
MaxScanSize 400M
StreamMaxLength 100M

The kiosk image also sets:

  • AlertEncrypted yes: an encrypted archive or document cannot be scanned; ClamAV reports it (Heuristics.Encrypted.Zip, .RAR, .PDF...) and the kiosk counts it as not fully scanned (error_names): the device is not verified, the file is not removed;
  • AlertOLE2Macros yes: an Office document with macros (VBA, also inside .docm or .xlsm) is suspicious (Heuristics.OLE2.ContainsMacros): with scan.suspicious = "block", it is quarantined and removed like a malicious file; "warn" only reports it.

Archives (zip, rar, 7z, tar, cab...) are unpacked and scanned by ClamAV itself, within its limits (MaxScanSize, MaxFileSize, MaxRecursion, MaxFiles): beyond them, a decompression bomb for instance, the file is not fully scanned (AlertExceedsMax).

ScanImageFuzzyHash no: ClamAV would decode every image, also those inside a PDF or an Office document, to compare a fuzzy hash with a few signatures of known images. It took half the scan time of a 29 MB PDF of images (41 s, then 19 s); the images are still scanned.

Files bigger than [engines.clamav] max_file_size are errors without being sent: keep it equal to the clamd limits.

Development setup (Debian or Ubuntu):

sudo apt install clamav-daemon clamav-freshclam
sudo systemctl stop clamav-freshclam && sudo freshclam && sudo systemctl start clamav-freshclam
# edit /etc/clamav/clamd.conf as above, then
sudo systemctl restart clamav-daemon

Third-party signatures (for example Sanesecurity) only need to be loadable by clamd: put the database files (.ndb, .hdb, .ldb...) in the clamd DatabaseDirectory (/var/lib/clamav) and reload clamd (clamdscan --reload). The upstream clamav-unofficial-sigs script automates this (the Debian package exists up to Debian 12 only). Some third-party signatures are prone to false positives: list their names in suspicious_names to report them as suspicious instead of malicious.

docs.title: YARA-X
docs.text:
YARA-X through its official Python bindings, with the YARA Forge and signature-base rules.

  • Rule sets ([engines.yara] rules): a list of { name, path }, where path is a .yar file or a folder of .yar/.yara files. Each file gets its own namespace, so identical rule names never conflict.
  • YARA Forge already includes signature-base: by default only the YARA Forge core package is configured. Add the full signature-base set only if you need the rules YARA Forge leaves out.
  • Compilation: once at startup. The compiled rules are cached in cache_dir, keyed by the YARA-X version, the options and the content of every rule file. The cache holds native code: it must be as trusted as the rules themselves (folder 0700, owned by the kiosk).
  • Compile errors are never silently dropped. on_compile_error = "fail" (default) refuses to start and lists every error; "skip_rule" drops the invalid rules, logs them and lists them in every scan report (engines[].extra.excluded_rules). exclude ignores rule files by glob pattern. With YARA-X 1.21, YARA Forge core (5,110 rules) and signature-base (5,904 rules) compile without error.
  • External variables used by the signature-base rules, filled for each file:
Variable Value filename file name filepath full path on the device, starting with / extension extension in lower case, with the dot (.exe) filetype THOR-like type mapped from the libmagic MIME type (EXE, ELF, ZIP, PDF...), empty when unknown: an approximation of THOR owner always empty: removable filesystems have no meaningful owner
  • Verdict mapping, from the score metadata of each matching rule (0-100, used by YARA Forge and signature-base):
Score Verdict >= malicious_score (75) malicious >= suspicious_score (40) suspicious below informational: recorded in the report (facts.informational), no effect on the verdict no score default_score (60): suspicious
  • Timeout: the native YARA-X timeout (timeout, seconds); a timeout is an error.
  • YARA-X compiles rules to native code at run time (wasmtime): it does not work under systemd MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes.

YARA does not unpack archives: EICAR inside a zip is detected by ClamAV, not by YARA.

docs.title: File type (libmagic)
docs.text: python-magic (Debian package python3-magic) identifies the MIME type and description from the first MiB of each file, given as a buffer: libmagic does not access the filesystem and does not decompress. The type is recorded in the report, used for the YARA filetype variable and by the heuristics.

docs.title: Heuristics
docs.text:
The structure of the files, without signatures (src/pandora_box/engines/heuristics.py, [engines.heuristics]); findings are suspicious, never malicious:

  • PDF with active content (like pdfid): JavaScript (/JavaScript, /JS) or a Launch action (Heuristics.PDF.JavaScript, Heuristics.PDF.Launch). Names hidden with escapes (/J#61vaScript) are decoded. Automatic actions, embedded files and forms (/OpenAction, /AA, /EmbeddedFile, /RichMedia, /XFA, /AcroForm) are counted as facts of the report. Names inside compressed object streams are not seen: ClamAV and YARA look there.
  • Disguised program: a program (PE, ELF, Mach-O, MSI, from libmagic) whose extension claims something else (facture.pdf: Heuristics.Executable.Disguised), or a document extension followed by one that Windows runs (facture.pdf.exe, rapport.docx.js: Heuristics.DoubleExtension).

The heuristics alone detect no malware: ClamAV or YARA-X stays required.

docs.title: Fake engine
docs.text: kiosk.fake_scan = true replaces every engine with the fake engine, for development only: it reports the EICAR test file as malicious and everything else as clean.

docs.title: File verdict
docs.text:
Engine results File verdict at least policy.min_malicious_engines engines report malicious (default: one) malicious otherwise, any malicious or suspicious result suspicious otherwise, any engine error or timeout, a content engine without result, or content engines skipped for another reason than a known file error otherwise clean

A file is never clean unless every enabled content engine scanned it, or skipped it because it is a known file.

docs.title: Device verdict
docs.text:
The worst file verdict: malicious, then suspicious, then not verified (a file could not be fully scanned, or the walk stopped at a limit), then clean. The kiosk then applies:

Setting block (default) warn scan.suspicious suspicious files are quarantined and removed like malicious ones they are kept and listed as a warning scan.on_error the device is reported as NOT VERIFIED: do not use it the user is warned

Files that could not be scanned are listed but never removed: they are not known to be malicious.

docs.title: Keys with several partitions
docs.text:
A key is scanned as a whole: all its partitions make one insertion, one verdict, one report and one confirmation. The kiosk mounts each filesystem in turn, read-only, and scans it; to clean the key, it mounts read-write only the partitions that hold the files to remove, then ejects the key once.

  • A key with a single filesystem, with or without a partition table, is scanned as before.
  • A partition that cannot be scanned is a reason of a not verified device (scan.on_error), as a computer may still read it: an encrypted partition (LUKS, BitLocker), a partition without a filesystem the kiosk recognizes, a filesystem that is not allowed (device.allowed_filesystems) or that cannot be mounted. Its other partitions are still scanned and cleaned. When none can be mounted, the kiosk shows an error.
  • Partitions that hold no files are ignored: MBR extended partitions (the container of the logical ones), GPT BIOS boot and Microsoft reserved partitions.
  • On the screen and in the report, a file is named after its partition (sdb2/docs/report.pdf). The report lists the partitions (device.partitions: filesystem, size, scanned or why not), and each file gives its partition, its path being relative to the root of that partition. The quarantine manifest gives the partition of each file too.
  • A maintenance, signature or image update device has a single filesystem: the folders of such a device are not looked for on a key with several partitions, which is scanned.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: Setting Default Beyond it limits.max_file_size 1 GiB the file is skipped, the device is not verified limits.max_files 100,000 files and folders; the walk stops, the device is not verified limits.max_depth 64 deeper folders are skipped, the device is not verified

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text:
Each worker process scans one file at a time. The kiosk process supervises them with two deadlines:

  • the engine deadline: the timeout of the running engine plus 5 seconds; engines with a native timeout (YARA-X, the clamd socket) report it first;
  • the file deadline: scan.file_timeout for the whole file.

When a deadline expires, the worker is killed and replaced, and the file is an error naming the engine. A crashed worker is handled the same way. A clean answer that arrives after the engine timeout is an error too.

docs.title: Signature freshness
docs.text: At startup, the kiosk warns (logs and screen) when a signature database is older than signatures.max_age_days (7 days), or the max_age_days of its engine (45 days for Hashlookup, published monthly). The date comes from the manifest.json of the signature folder when present ({"<file>": {"version", "date", "source", "sha256"}}), otherwise from the file modification time; ClamAV reports its own database date. A database without a date is only logged (signatures_undated), not shown: a ClamAV database of custom signatures only has none (the date comes from the header of the official daily database).

docs.title: Scan report
docs.text: Every scan writes a JSON report in report.folder, described by src/pandora_box/schemas/scan-report-v1.schema.json: device, configuration, engines and signature versions, every file with its hashes, type, verdict and per-engine results, the device verdict and the actions taken. The quarantine manifest references it.

docs.title: Reference hardware
docs.text: A kiosk is a refurbished Lenovo ThinkCentre Tiny with a 7-inch touchscreen. The image runs on any x86_64 UEFI computer, but only the hardware below is validated: the image sets the mode of its screen and allows its touchscreen (see image.md).

docs.title: Validated hardware
docs.text:
Part Model Notes Computer Lenovo ThinkCentre M720q Tiny (machine type 10T7), BIOS M1UKT62A Core i5-9400T (6 cores), Intel UHD Graphics 630, 8 GB, SATA SSD 128 GB Screen Waveshare 7-inch HDMI LCD (C), 1024x600, capacitive touch HDMI for the picture, USB for the touch controller 0eef:0005 "WS170120"

What was checked on it: Secure Boot with the image key, boot and A/B updates, the screen (all of the interface visible), the touchscreen (confirms a cleaning), USB keys, detection (EICAR), online updates of the signatures over the wired network, maintenance devices.

Notes for this hardware:

  • Screen: the firmware starts in 1024x768 and the Intel driver keeps that framebuffer; the kernel command line sets the mode of the screen (video=1024x600M@60) and the kiosk shrinks the console to it.
  • Touchscreen: USBGuard allows its touch controller by its identifiers, serial number and port (1-8, where it is connected inside the enclosure): image/mkosi.extra/etc/usbguard/rules.conf. Another unit or another port: change the rule, as shown by usb-devices.txt of a maintenance export, or by the audit log of USBGuard when it blocks it.
  • Graphics firmware: the image has no firmware for the Intel graphics (the DMC firmware of Coffee Lake): the display works, without its deepest power saving states.
  • Speed: about 0.5 s per MB for a PDF full of images (ClamAV), much less for other files (ClamAV takes almost all of it); six files are scanned at the same time, one per core.

A computer or a screen not listed here may need its own settings: the mode of its screen, the rule of its touchscreen, the disk controller in the initrd (KernelModulesInitrdInclude= of image/mkosi.conf: NVMe, SATA, Intel VMD, eMMC).

docs.title: Enclosure
docs.text: A 3D-printed desk enclosure, one part, about 191 x 184 x 86 mm: the screen in the window of its tilted front face, ventilation slots on its rounded back. The model and its views are in 3D/, under the CERN Open Hardware Licence v2 - Strongly Reciprocal (CERN-OHL-S v2).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: The BIOS settings of the M720q, the writing of the image and the first boot are described in Initial installation.

docs.title: Image internals
docs.text:
How the kiosk image is made and protected. To build it, test it, install it and maintain it, see Building the image, Testing with QEMU, Initial installation and System updates.

The image is built with mkosi from Debian 13 (trixie) packages.

docs.title: Partitions
docs.text:
The disk image has two system slots (A/B updates) and a data partition:

Partition Filesystem Content ESP vfat, 512 MB systemd-boot and the UKIs (pandora-box_<version>.efi), all signed root, slot A (pandora-box_<version>) EROFS, read-only, 1 GB the whole system but /var (about 400 MB used) root-verity, slot A 64 MB dm-verity hash tree of the root filesystem root-verity-sig, slot A 16 KB signature of the root hash root, root-verity, root-verity-sig, slot B (_empty) same sizes the next version (A/B updates) data (pandora-box-data) ext4, 1 GB in the image /var: scan reports, quarantine, logs, signed signature sets (clamd reads its databases there)

The version of the image is the date and time of its build, UTC, like the serial of a signature set: 20261005143700 (image/build.sh sets it, --image-version=N overrides it). It is in /etc/os-release (IMAGE_VERSION), in the labels of its partitions (pandora-box_<version>, _verity, _veritysig: 36 characters at most) and in the name of its UKI.

The root filesystem is read-only by design (EROFS cannot be written at all): the system and its configuration only change with a new image. Everything the kiosk writes is in /var. The data partition is the last one: at every boot, systemd-repart grows it to fill the disk (/usr/lib/repart.d/20-var.conf), then systemd-growfs grows its filesystem (x-systemd.growfs in /etc/fstab), so the image can be written to a disk of any size. As /etc is read-only, the machine ID is generated again at every boot (a new journal folder per boot, within the journald size limits).

The image contains:

  • the kernel, systemd and udev, Python 3 and clamd (clamav-daemon), with no network service: systemd-networkd, systemd-resolved, freshclam and the ClamAV on-access scanner are disabled (10-pandora-box.preset);
  • pandora-box in /usr/lib/pandora-box (/usr/bin/pandora-box), its configuration in /etc/pandora-box/pandora-box.toml and its service, which shows the curses interface on the first console;
  • no login program and no root password: no interactive session is possible.

docs.title: Signing, Secure Boot and dm-verity
docs.text:
The boot chain is verified from the firmware to every block of the system:

  1. with Secure Boot, the firmware only starts systemd-boot if it is signed with a key of its db, and systemd-boot only starts a signed UKI;
  2. the UKI holds the kernel, the initrd and the kernel command line, which contains the dm-verity root hash (roothash=): changing it breaks the signature;
  3. the root filesystem is opened with dm-verity: every block read is checked against the hash tree, whose root is that hash. A modified block cannot be read (I/O error, "data block ... is corrupted" in the kernel log);
  4. with Secure Boot, the Debian kernel enables its lockdown mode (integrity): even root cannot modify the running kernel.

/var is not protected by dm-verity: it holds the data of the kiosk, never programs or configuration.

The image is signed with image/mkosi.key and image/mkosi.crt (systemd-boot, UKI, root hash). When they do not exist, image/build.sh generates a development key pair, valid 10 years, that never leaves the developer's computer (ignored by git). A kiosk must only trust the release keys of the project, which are not defined yet: they will be kept out of the repository, and mkosi can sign with a key in a hardware token (--secure-boot-key-source=provider:pkcs11).

The image also trusts the signature sets signed with image/update.key: its public key image/update.pem is installed in /usr/share/pandora-box/keys/ (under dm-verity). image/build.sh generates a development pair when they do not exist; the test profile signs its signature set with it. See Signatures.

On a kiosk, the certificate is enrolled in the firmware in place of the Microsoft keys (PK, KEK and db), so that it starts nothing else. The ESP contains the keys in the format expected by the firmware (loader/keys/auto/): with the firmware in Secure Boot setup mode (keys cleared in the firmware setup), systemd-boot enrolls them at the first boot (secure-boot-enroll force). Enrolling only the project certificate also refuses the option ROMs signed by Microsoft: a computer whose display or disk controller needs one (a graphics card, for instance) would not start it. The virtual machines enroll the certificate with virt-fw-vars instead (image/vm/machine.py).

systemd-boot has no menu (/efi/loader/loader.conf, timeout menu-disabled): it starts the default entry, the newest version not marked bad, and does not read the keyboard. A keyboard plugged into the kiosk cannot select another version, edit the kernel command line (refused with Secure Boot anyway), power off the machine or reboot into the firmware setup. The ESP is not part of the image updates: this file stays as installed.

docs.title: Screen
docs.text:
The kiosk draws its graphical interface into the framebuffer of the graphics driver (/dev/fb0), without a display server or a browser, and puts the first console (tty1) in graphics mode so that the kernel does not draw text over it: see interface.md. The screen of the reference hardware is a Waveshare 7-inch HDMI LCD (1024x600). The firmware of the ThinkCentre starts in 1024x768, and the Intel driver keeps that mode: the bottom of the interface would be off the screen. The kernel command line therefore sets the mode of the screen, video=1024x600M@60 (CVT timings, as Waveshare documents them); with another screen, change it in image/mkosi.conf. The Intel driver still keeps the framebuffer of the firmware, large enough for that mode: the kiosk only draws its visible part, the size of video=, and follows a change of the framebuffer size. It logs the size and the pixel format it draws for (display_started).

The curses interface (kiosk.interface = "curses", administrator mode) draws text on the console instead: it shrinks the console to the screen of video= (8x16 font: 37 lines, 128 columns) the same way, and logs the size it draws for (display_started, display_resized).

docs.title: USB devices
docs.text:
A kiosk must only use USB storage devices: a key that is also a keyboard (BadUSB) could type commands, a network adapter could open a network.

  • USBGuard (/etc/usbguard/rules.conf) allows hubs and the devices whose interfaces are all mass storage; it blocks every other device, including a key that has a storage interface and another one. Blocked devices are listed in /var/log/usbguard/usbguard-audit.log.
  • No device is authorized before USBGuard has started: the kernel command line sets usbcore.authorized_default=0. If USBGuard does not start, no USB device is usable.
  • Drivers removed from the image (KernelModulesExclude= in image/mkosi.conf): USB network adapters, wireless, Bluetooth, USB serial adapters and modems, plus the staging drivers and batman-adv, which would bring the wireless modules back as dependencies. Such devices have no driver even if they were authorized.
  • USB HID is kept for the touchscreen of the reference hardware, a Waveshare 7-inch HDMI LCD (C), allowed by its own rule:
allow id 0eef:0005 serial "220211" name "WS170120" with-interface 03:00:00 via-port "1-8"

its USB touch controller (eGalax) with its single generic HID interface (a keyboard has 03:01:01), on the internal port of the enclosure, this unit only. A device that copies its identifiers on another port, or that adds a keyboard interface, is blocked; so is every keyboard and mouse. Another unit or port: adapt the rule to the line the audit log shows when it is blocked. The kernel (mousedev) turns a touch into a left click on /dev/input/mice, which the kiosk reads to confirm a cleaning.

The test image allows the touch tablet of the virtual machine (QEMU usb-tablet, same interface) in its own rule (/etc/usbguard/rules.d/50-vm-test.conf): the test confirms a cleaning with a touch. The keyboard of the virtual machines is not a USB device.

docs.title: System hardening
docs.text:
After the ANSSI configuration recommendations for GNU/Linux systems:

  • Kernel settings (/usr/lib/sysctl.d/90-pandora-box.conf): kernel logs and addresses hidden, no ptrace, no kexec, no unprivileged eBPF, user namespaces or userfaultfd, io_uring disabled, no SysRq, no core dumps, protected links and FIFOs, no IP forwarding or redirects.
  • Kernel command line: memory initialized on allocation and free, no slab merging, randomized page allocator and kernel stack, no legacy vsyscall, no debugfs, lockdown in confidentiality mode (Secure Boot only enables integrity: even root cannot read kernel memory), IOMMU in strict mode and no DMA before the kernel starts (DMA attacks through ports).
  • Firewall (/etc/nftables.conf): every packet is dropped, in and out, except on the loopback interface.
  • No login: no login console on the screens (getty@ and getty-static disabled), no login program, no root password, Ctrl-Alt-Del masked.
  • clamd sandbox (clamav-daemon.service.d/50-pandora-box.conf): no network, read-only system, no device, system call filter, MemoryDenyWriteExecute (the Debian clamd interprets bytecode signatures, without JIT); it runs as the clamav user.
  • Kiosk service (packaging/systemd/pandora-box.service): read-only system, system call filter, limited capabilities. It keeps AF_NETLINK (udev events), the capabilities needed to start the worker sandbox (namespaces, change of user, loopback interface of the workers) and cannot have MemoryDenyWriteExecute or RestrictSUIDSGID: the first one would also apply to the YARA-X workers, which compile rules to native code, the second one refuses a system call bubblewrap needs.
  • Kernel modules removed: network protocols the kiosk never uses (DCCP, SCTP, RDS, TIPC) and FireWire, another way to reach the memory of the kiosk, besides the USB network, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi drivers. The protocols and FireWire are also listed in /etc/modprobe.d/pandora-box.conf, where the auditing tools look for them.
  • Audit log (/etc/audit/audit.rules, auditd): loading of kernel modules, mounts (except those of systemd and bubblewrap), every program started, ptrace, changes of the clock, of the signature sets and of the staged image updates. The rules are locked (-e 2): changing them needs a reboot. They are loaded by auditctl -R (augenrules writes into /etc, read-only). The log is in /var/log/audit/audit.log, for instance ausearch -k signatures -i.

The test profile includes lynis, run by the automated test: hardening index 73, no warnings. Its remaining suggestions do not apply to a kiosk without login (password policy, banners, package tools, fail2ban) or come later (remote logging, phase 5).

docs.title: Scan worker sandbox
docs.text:
The scan workers parse hostile files with several engines (libmagic, YARA-X, the clamd client...): they are assumed compromisable (scan.sandbox, src/pandora_box/sandbox.py).

  • One engine per worker: a compromised engine (a crafted file exploiting YARA-X or libmagic) cannot forge the result of another engine. The kiosk hashes each file itself, asks the worker of each hash engine (MalwareBazaar, Hashlookup) with the hashes only, then passes the file to a worker of each content engine (ClamAV, YARA-X), and combines their results itself; a worker only reports the result of its own engine. Content engines have scan.workers workers each, hash engines one. scan.workers = "auto" (the default) scans one file per CPU at the same time, as many as the memory allows (1.5 GB for clamd and the system, then 256 MB each, for the YARA rules mostly): 6 on the ThinkCentre M720q (6 cores, 8 GB), 1 or 2 on a computer with 2 GB.
  • No access to the device: the kiosk opens each file safely (no link followed, the file of the inventory) and passes the open descriptor to the workers of the content engines, which never open a file of the device; the workers of the hash engines never get the file.
  • bubblewrap: new PID, IPC, UTS, cgroup and network namespaces (no network interface but loopback); a file system holding only /usr, a few files of /etc, the signature folders of the enabled engines (read-only), the YARA-X cache and the clamd socket folder: no device mount point, no reports, quarantine, logs or configuration.
  • Dedicated user pandora-box-scan (packaging/sysusers/), switched to by setpriv: no capability, no supplementary group, no_new_privs.
  • System call filter (src/pandora_box/seccomp.py), installed once the engines are loaded: no program execution, debugging, mounts, namespaces, eBPF, kernel modules, io_uring, network sockets...
  • Untrusted answers: workers answer in JSON (never pickle), limited in size and validated (src/pandora_box/protocol.py); the path and size of the file always come from the kiosk. A malformed answer kills the worker and the file is reported as an error.

bubblewrap runs as root (the kiosk service), so unprivileged user namespaces stay disabled.

The virtual machine test checks these settings and prints the exposure of the services measured by systemd-analyze security (0 to 10, lower is better): about 1.6 for clamd, 3.8 for the kiosk (which starts the worker sandbox), 2.8 for USBGuard.

docs.title: Unified kernel image
docs.text: The UKI (about 40 MB) holds the kernel, the initrd of the image (image/mkosi.images/initrd/, without the udev hardware database, charset conversions, Perl, documentation and networkd) and an initrd of kernel modules. That one only holds what mounts the root filesystem (KernelModulesInitrdInclude= in image/mkosi.conf): disk controllers (NVMe, SATA, Intel VMD, eMMC, virtio), dm-verity, EROFS and CRC32C, which EROFS loads by name. The other modules are loaded from the root filesystem. A computer whose disk controller is not in this list cannot find its root filesystem: add its module there.

docs.title: Initial installation
docs.text: A kiosk is installed once: the BIOS is configured, the image is written to its disk, Secure Boot is locked to the image key at the first boot, then a first signature set is installed from a USB key. Afterwards it is only updated with signed USB keys or online (Maintenance).

docs.title: In short
docs.text:
1. Build the image: Building the image.
  2. Configure the BIOS: supervisor password, Secure Boot in setup mode, boot from the internal disk only.
  3. Write the image to the disk of the kiosk.
  4. First boot: the image enrolls its Secure Boot key; check that Secure Boot is in User mode.
  5. Insert a first signature set: until then, the kiosk shows NO VALID SIGNATURES and scans nothing.
  6. Check the kiosk with a test key and a maintenance device.

The settings below are those of the validated hardware, a Lenovo ThinkCentre M720q Tiny (see Hardware).

docs.title: BIOS configuration
docs.text: The settings of the ThinkCentre M720q (press F1 at power on). The names are those of the Lenovo BIOS of this generation and may vary slightly with the version; the goal of each setting matters more than its exact name.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Setting Value Why Security → Supervisor Password set, kept by the operator nobody changes the boot order, Secure Boot or the settings below Security → Power-On Password none the kiosk starts by itself after a power failure Security → Secure Boot → Secure Boot Enabled the firmware only starts the signed boot loader of the image Security → Secure Boot → Secure Boot Mode Custom, then Reset to Setup Mode (or Clear All Secure Boot Keys) at its first boot, the image enrolls its own certificate (loader/keys/auto): the computer then only starts PandoraBox images Security → Device Guard / Intel TXT default not used Security → Chassis Intrusion Detection Enabled, if the enclosure has the switch an opened kiosk is reported at the next start

Enrolling only the image certificate also refuses the option ROMs signed by Microsoft: fine with the integrated Intel graphics of the M720q, but a computer that needs an add-in graphics card or disk controller would not start it.

docs.title: Startup
docs.text: Setting Value Why Startup → Boot Mode UEFI only the image only boots in UEFI mode Startup → Primary Boot Sequence the internal SSD only the kiosk never starts from a USB key inserted by a user Startup → USB Boot Disabled same Startup → PXE / Network Boot Disabled no start from the network Startup → Boot Menu (F12) Disabled, if offered no other boot device chosen at power on (the supervisor password protects it otherwise) Startup → Fast Boot default

docs.title: Devices and advanced settings
docs.text: Setting Value Why Advanced → CPU Setup → Intel Virtualization Technology for Directed I/O (VT-d) Enabled the IOMMU protects the memory against DMA from devices (the kernel uses it in strict mode) Devices → Network Setup → Wake on LAN Disabled Devices → USB Setup the ports not used by the users or the touchscreen disabled, if the BIOS offers it per port fewer ways in (physical hardening) Devices → Audio / Serial / Card reader Disabled when present not used

docs.title: Power
docs.text: Setting Value Why Power → After Power Loss Power On the kiosk starts again after a power failure

docs.title: Writing the image
docs.text:
The SSD is written once, from another computer (in a USB enclosure), with the build container:

lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,MODEL,TRAN          # the disk of the SSD, e.g. /dev/sdX
docker run --rm --device /dev/sdX -v "$PWD/image/mkosi.output:/o:ro" \
    pandora-box-builder dd if=/o/pandora-box.raw of=/dev/sdX bs=4M conv=fsync status=progress

Caution

Check the disk name twice: dd overwrites the whole disk.

The image can be written to a disk of any size: at every boot, the data partition (/var) grows to fill the disk.

docs.title: First boot
docs.text:
Put the SSD back in the kiosk and start it. With the firmware in Secure Boot setup mode, systemd-boot enrolls the certificate of the image in place of the Microsoft keys (PK, KEK and db, from loader/keys/auto/ on the ESP), then the kiosk starts. From then on, the computer only starts images signed with the same key.

After this first boot, check in the BIOS that Secure Boot is on: it shows the mode User. To give the computer back to another use: Security → Secure Boot → Restore Factory Keys.

The boot loader has no menu and does not read the keyboard: there is no way to choose another system or to open a session on the kiosk.

docs.title: First signature set
docs.text:
A new kiosk has no signature set: it shows NO VALID SIGNATURES and only accepts a signature update device. Prepare one on the computer that holds the update key, and insert it (see Signatures):

export ABUSECH_AUTH_KEY=...
publish/publish.sh /srv/pandora-box/pandora-box-signatures image/update.key
cp -r /srv/pandora-box/pandora-box-signatures /media/$USER/KEY/

The kiosk verifies and installs the set, loads its engines, asks to remove the key, then waits for a key to scan. A kiosk built with the profile online and connected to the network also downloads its signatures itself, 5 minutes after boot (Online updates).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Insert a key holding the EICAR test file: the kiosk reports it, and removes it after a touch of the screen.
  • The touchscreen confirms a cleaning. If it does not, USBGuard blocks it: its rule is tied to the serial number and port of the touch controller (USB devices).
  • Bring the logs back with a maintenance device: failed-services.txt is empty, signatures.txt shows the installed set.

docs.title: Kiosk interface
docs.text:
The kiosk shows what it does on its touch screen: waiting for a key, scan progress, the dangerous files found, then the result. There are no buttons: the only action of the user is a touch anywhere on the screen to start the cleaning, once the files to remove are listed.

Waiting for a key Scan in progress Threats found: touch to clean Key cleaned

docs.title: Screens
docs.text:
Screen When ready Waiting for a key (animation of a key inserted), with the versions of the kiosk and of its signatures unavailable No valid signatures: the kiosk only accepts a signature update device scanning Device, progress bar, files scanned out of the total, threats found so far, the latest files scanned and their verdict threats The files that will be removed, with their detection; a touch on the screen cleans the key cleaning The files being removed clean No threat found: the key can be used warning Suspicious or not fully scanned files are kept (scan.suspicious or scan.on_error set to warn) cleaned The removed files not_cleaned The files that could not be removed, or the key was removed before the cleaning not_verified Files that could not be scanned (scan.on_error = "block"): the key must not be used error The key could not be mounted or read service Maintenance, signature or image update device: the messages of the kiosk

A result (scan, maintenance or update device) stays on the screen until the key is removed, then display.return_seconds more (5 seconds by default) before the waiting screen. Inserting another key shows its scan at once.

docs.title: How it is drawn
docs.text:
The screens are drawn with Pillow and copied into the Linux framebuffer (display.framebuffer, /dev/fb0): no display server, no browser, nothing that listens on a socket. The kiosk puts its console (tty1) in graphics mode, so that the kernel does not draw text over the screens. Touches are read from /dev/input/mice (the touch screen is seen as a mouse), only while the kiosk waits for the cleaning to be confirmed. File names and device labels come from the key: they are made printable (control and invisible formatting characters replaced) and cut to their place, never interpreted. The graphical interface needs a 24 or 32 bits per pixel framebuffer (Intel, efifb, QEMU).

The configuration selects it with kiosk.interface = "framebuffer" (the default); curses is the text interface (administrator mode), console prints plain text (development).

docs.title: Customization
docs.text: An administrator adapts the interface to the organization: logo, colors, texts of every screen and their language, images. The image is read-only (dm-verity): the theme is part of it, and a change needs a new image (or an image update).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
In packaging/pandora-box.toml, section [display]:

[display]
# Theme folder, installed in the image from image/theme/
theme = "/usr/share/pandora-box/theme"
# Language of the texts: "en", "fr", or a language the theme adds
language = "fr"
# Seconds before the waiting screen, once the key is removed
return_seconds = 5.0

docs.title: Theme folder
docs.text:
Create image/theme/ in the repository: the image build copies it to /usr/share/pandora-box/theme and checks it (the build fails on an invalid theme). The folder holds a theme.toml and the files it names. Every key is optional: a key of the theme replaces the one of the built-in theme (src/pandora_box/ui/theme/theme.toml, which lists them all), the others are kept.

image/theme/
├── theme.toml
└── logo.png

# Logo of the organization, on the left of the header (PNG or JPEG)
logo = "logo.png"
# TrueType fonts, files of the folder (default: DejaVu Sans)
# font = "OpenSans-Regular.ttf"
# font_bold = "OpenSans-Bold.ttf"

[colors]
header = "#003366"
progress = "#003366"

[texts.fr]
title = "Hôpital de Mons - Borne antivirus"
footer = "Service informatique - poste 1234"
insert_help = "Analysez toute clé USB avant de l'utiliser sur un poste de l'hôpital."
clean_help = "Cette clé peut être utilisée. N'oubliez pas de la retirer."

docs.title: Texts
docs.text:
Every text shown on the screen is a key of [texts.<language>]: the title of the header, the footer, the title and the help of each screen, the verdicts of the files. Some texts have placeholders, replaced by the kiosk:

Text Placeholders scan_progress {done}, {total} scan_threats, cleaned_help, more_files {count} device_usage {size}, {used}

A text with an unknown placeholder or an unknown key is refused. A theme may add a language: [texts.de] with the texts it translates, the others are in English; then set display.language = "de".

The messages of the service, error, unavailable and cleaning screens are those of the kiosk logs (in English): they are meant for the administrator, and are not part of the theme.

docs.title: Colors
docs.text: header, header_text, background, text, muted (help, details), clean, threat, warning, progress, progress_background: "#rrggbb".

docs.title: Images
docs.text: [images]: insert (animation of the waiting screen, one image per second), busy (animation while the kiosk works), clean, threat, error (icons of the results). PNG (with transparency) or JPEG, at most 4096 pixels. The built-in images come from the first version of PandoraBox.

docs.title: Check and preview a theme
docs.text:
Without a kiosk, on the development computer:

pandora-box-theme check image/theme
pandora-box-theme preview image/theme /tmp/preview            # every language
pandora-box-theme preview image/theme /tmp/preview --language fr --size 800x480

preview draws every screen, with made-up files, into PNG files. pandora-box --check-config also checks the theme of the configuration.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text: A kiosk has no login and accepts no connection: its logs are brought back with a signed maintenance device, or sent as they are logged to a SIEM by an online kiosk.

docs.title: In short
docs.text:
image/maintenance-key.sh /media/$USER/KEY            # any kiosk
image/maintenance-key.sh /media/$USER/KEY kiosk-1    # only kiosk.name = kiosk-1

Insert the key into the kiosk: it writes its logs to pandora-box-maintenance/<kiosk>-<date>/ and ejects the key.

For a continuous export, see Log export to a SIEM.

docs.title: What the kiosk logs
docs.text:
Log Path on the kiosk Content Kiosk /var/log/pandora-box/pandora-box.log JSON lines: devices inserted and removed, scans and their verdicts, infected files, quarantine and cleaning, signature and image updates, maintenance devices, errors Scan reports /var/lib/pandora-box/reports/ One JSON report per scanned device (see Scan report) Quarantine /var/lib/pandora-box/quarantine/ Copies of the infected files removed from the keys Journal journalctl System, services and kernel; one folder per boot, within the journald size limits USBGuard /var/log/usbguard/usbguard-audit.log Devices allowed and blocked Audit /var/log/audit/audit.log Kernel modules loaded, mounts, programs started, ptrace, changes of the clock, of the signature sets and of the staged image updates

Every entry of the kiosk log holds timestamp, level, kiosk (kiosk.name) and event, then the fields of the event. The level is set by logging.level (INFO by default). logrotate moves the log file every month and keeps 12 months, compressed.

Everything is on the data partition (/var), kept across reboots and image updates.

docs.title: Maintenance device
docs.text:
A maintenance device brings the logs of a kiosk back without taking its disk out. On the computer that holds the update key, with a USB key mounted:

image/maintenance-key.sh /media/$USER/KEY            # any kiosk
image/maintenance-key.sh /media/$USER/KEY kiosk-1    # only kiosk.name = kiosk-1

writes pandora-box-maintenance/ on the key: a request signed with the update key, valid 7 days. Inserted into the kiosk, even one without signatures, the key is not scanned: the kiosk verifies the request, writes its logs to pandora-box-maintenance/<kiosk>-<date>/ and ejects the key (src/pandora_box/maintenance.py).

File Content pandora-box.log Log of the kiosk journal.txt, journal-previous-boot.txt Journal of the boot and of the previous one kernel.txt Kernel messages boots.txt, boot-entries.txt Boots, installed versions of the image (System updates) services.txt, failed-services.txt systemd units, failed units usbguard-audit.log, usb-devices.txt, usb-rules.txt USB devices allowed and blocked, rules disks.txt Disks and partitions hardware.txt, cpuinfo.txt, meminfo.txt, input-devices.txt Hardware and screens, input devices os-release.txt, cmdline.txt Version of the image, kernel command line signatures.txt Installed signature set

Nothing changes on the kiosk, and the export holds no key, credential or scan report. A request signed by another key, too old, for another kiosk or modified is refused (maintenance_refused in the log).

One key can hold a maintenance request, a signature set (pandora-box-signatures/) and an image update (pandora-box-image/): the kiosk handles them in that order in one insertion, each verified on its own; the export shows the kiosk before the updates, and the image update comes last as it restarts the kiosk.

docs.title: Useful events
docs.text: Event Meaning device_verdict Verdict of a scanned device infected_files Dangerous files found on a device signatures_installed, signatures_refused, signatures_not_newer Result of a signature update device signatures_changed New signature set loaded after an online update maintenance_refused Maintenance request refused display_started, display_resized Size of the screen the interface draws for

docs.title: Export to a SIEM
docs.text: An online kiosk can send every entry of its log to a SIEM (Wazuh, Elastic, Graylog, Splunk, or any syslog server), over syslog or JSON, TLS, TCP or UDP: see Log export to a SIEM.

docs.title: Log export to a SIEM
docs.text: The kiosk logs every event to a JSON lines file, /var/log/pandora-box/pandora-box.log: devices inserted and removed, scans and their verdicts, infected files, quarantine and cleaning, signature and image updates, maintenance devices, errors. An online kiosk can send these entries to a SIEM (Wazuh, Elastic, Graylog, Splunk, or any syslog server), as they are logged.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The export is off by default. It needs the image profile online (Building the image), which brings the network and the pandora-box-siem service, and the [siem] section of the configuration (packaging/pandora-box.toml):

[siem]
enabled = true
host = "siem.example.org"
# "tls" (default), "tcp" or "udp"
transport = "tls"
# 0: 6514 for tls, 514 for tcp and udp
port = 0
# Certificate authorities of the SIEM certificate, for tls ("": those of the
# system)
ca = "/usr/share/pandora-box/siem-ca.pem"
# "syslog" (RFC 5424) or "json"
format = "syslog"
facility = "local0"

pandora-box --check-config checks the section. The certificate authorities are part of the image: put them in image/siem-ca.pem (PEM), installed as /usr/share/pandora-box/siem-ca.pem when the image is built.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
Each log entry is one message.

format = "syslog": an RFC 5424 message whose header comes from the entry, and whose message is the JSON entry itself:

<132>1 2026-10-14T10:25:32.123456+00:00 kiosk-01 pandora-box - infected_files - {"timestamp": "2026-10-14T10:25:32.123456+00:00", "level": "WARNING", "kiosk": "kiosk-01", "event": "infected_files", "count": 2}
